name: Chung Ha (청하)
basis: Long-running mass-market cheongju; specs from Lotte Chilsung public product information.
tastingNotes: Korea's everyday clear rice wine — light, softly sweet, with a gentle savory depth that will remind you of a mild sake. Served cold, it is clean and easy, with none of soju's alcohol bite.

specs.label: Style
specs.value: Cheongju — Korea's clear rice wine, cousin to Japanese sake

history.event: Chung Ha launches and becomes the standard restaurant cheongju nationwide.

story: Walk into any Korean raw-fish restaurant and the green-labeled bottle chilling next to the soju is Chung Ha. Cheongju is Korea's own clear rice wine tradition — the ancestor category that royal courts drank — and this is its approachable, modern mass-market face. For newcomers it is the gentlest possible introduction to Korean rice alcohol.
winery: Lotte Chilsung Beverage, one of Korea's largest drinks companies, has produced Chung Ha since the 1980s.

foodPairing.why: The classic — clean rice wine and fresh raw fish is Korea's answer to sake and sashimi.
Light sweetness complements the shellfish without covering it.
Soft umami on umami — a comfortable, low-intensity match.

pairingTip: Anywhere you would order sake, Chung Ha fits — especially raw fish and light seafood.
avoidPairing: Heavy red-spice dishes like buldak overwhelm its delicate profile completely.
trivia: Many Koreans' first not-soju drink at a family dinner is Chung Ha — it is considered polite enough for drinking with grandparents.
servingNote: Served cold in small ceramic or glass cups; in restaurants it often arrives in an ice bucket. Pour for others first, as always.
aging: Not for aging — drink fresh; refrigerate after opening and finish within a few days.
tips: If you like it, graduate to craft yakju like Pungjeong Sagye — same family, deeper flavors
It also warms gently well in winter, sake-style

name: Gapyeong Jat Makgeolli (가평 잣 생막걸리)
basis: Woorisool's flagship regional product; Gapyeong's pine nut fame is well documented.
tastingNotes: A fresh, milky rice makgeolli enriched with pine nuts from Gapyeong, Korea's pine nut capital. The nuts add a subtle creamy richness and faint sweetness on top of the usual gentle fizz and yogurt-like tang. One of the most crowd-pleasing regional makgeollis.

specs.label: Base
specs.value: Rice, nuruk (Korean fermentation starter), Gapyeong pine nuts

history.event: Woorisool grows into one of Korea's largest makgeolli producers, building its identity on Gapyeong pine nuts.

story: Gapyeong, a mountain county east of Seoul, is where Koreans go for pine-nut everything — and its makgeolli is the edible souvenir. Woorisool blends local pine nuts into a fresh rice brew, giving the rustic farmer's drink a nutty, almost dessert-like touch. It is a staple at the region's riverside chicken restaurants.
winery: Woorisool, based in Gapyeong, is among Korea's biggest makgeolli breweries, exporting widely while keeping its pine-nut flagship rooted in local agriculture.

foodPairing.why: Makgeolli and pajeon on a rainy day is a national ritual — the fizz cuts the oil.
Creamy nuttiness soothes the gochujang heat — the classic Gapyeong combo.
Nut on nut — it amplifies the drink's signature flavor.

pairingTip: Anything fried or spicy works; the drink behaves like a gentle, fizzy cream to cool things down.
avoidPairing: Delicate raw fish — the milky body and tang smother it.
trivia: Gapyeong supplies a large share of Korea's pine nuts, and locals insist the makgeolli tastes best within sight of the mountains that grew them.
servingNote: Gently invert the bottle two or three times before opening to mix the settled rice sediment — never shake hard, it will fizz over. Drink from small bowls, not glasses, for the full experience.
aging: Unpasteurized and alive: refrigerate always, drink within about two weeks of bottling, and expect the taste to get more sour and fizzy by the day.
tips: The date on the cap is the bottling date — fresher is milder, older is tangier
Pour the last cloudy third in too; that sediment is where the flavor lives

name: Nimome (니모메)
basis: Jeju Saemju's flagship yakju; tangerine peel infusion and Jeju-dialect name are the brand's public identity.
tastingNotes: A refined rice wine from Jeju Island infused with dried tangerine peel from the island's famous orchards. Expect a softly sweet, faintly citrus-fragrant sip that finishes clean — like sunshine over a traditional yakju. Dangerously easy to drink.

specs.label: Base
specs.value: Rice, nuruk (fermentation starter), Jeju tangerine peel

history.event: Jeju Saemju is founded to modernize Jeju's brewing traditions.

story: The name means 'in your heart' in Jeju dialect, and the drink is exactly that kind of souvenir: the island's beloved tangerines, folded into a traditional rice wine. It has become the bottle travelers bring back from Jeju when they want something more special than airport chocolate.
winery: Jeju Saemju is a Jeju Island brewery known for weaving local ingredients — tangerine peel, Jeju water, island grains — into approachable traditional alcohol.

foodPairing.why: Citrus lift against rich grilled pork is the island's own pairing.
Tangerine on tangerine — it reads like a light dessert wine.
The gentle sweetness complements rather than covers.

pairingTip: Serve it chilled as an aperitif or with lighter food; it also makes a lovely low-proof nightcap.
avoidPairing: Deep-fried, heavily sauced dishes bury the delicate citrus note.
trivia: Jeju has its own dialect that mainland Koreans struggle to understand — putting Nimome on the label was a deliberate act of island pride.
servingNote: Chill well and serve in small clear glasses to show off the pale gold color; a citrus-peel garnish is fair play.
aging: Not for aging; keep refrigerated after opening and finish within a week or two.
tips: A great gift bottle — light enough for people who do not usually drink traditional alcohol
Works in a spritz with sparkling water on summer evenings

name: Sansachun (산사춘)
basis: Long-selling Baesangmyun Juga brand; hawthorn (sansa) base is its defining public trait.
tastingNotes: A honey-gold rice wine flavored with sansa — hawthorn berries — giving it a sweet-tart, faintly fruity character unlike anything in Western wine. Smooth and lightly warming, it drinks like a gentle berry mead with Korean roots.

history.event: Baesangmyun Juga launches Sansachun, which becomes a fixture of Korean restaurant menus.

story: Hawthorn berries have been used in Korean herbal tradition for centuries, prized for helping digestion — which is exactly how Sansachun is drunk: alongside rich, meaty dinners. Its poetic name means spring of the hawthorn, and for many Koreans it was the first traditional alcohol that felt approachable rather than old-fashioned.
winery: Baesangmyun Juga is a family brewing house dedicated to reviving traditional Korean alcohol; the founding family also created the Neurin Maeul makgeolli brand.

foodPairing.why: Sweet-tart berry notes echo the soy-sugar marinade beautifully.
Fruit wine and rich duck is a pairing that crosses every culture.
Gentle sweetness matches the sesame-soy noodles.

pairingTip: Think of it where you would pour an off-dry rosé: grilled marinated meat, festive family tables.
avoidPairing: Very sour dishes like naengmyeon with extra vinegar clash with its fruit acidity.
trivia: TV dramas of the 2000s made a glass of Sansachun shorthand for a warm family dinner scene.
servingNote: Serve lightly chilled in small glasses; it is a mealtime wine, meant to be topped up for everyone through dinner.
aging: Shelf-stable unopened; refrigerate after opening and enjoy within a few weeks.
tips: A safe first bottle for guests who find soju too harsh and makgeolli too funky
Over ice with a squeeze of lemon it becomes an easy aperitif
